lead: Road and rail alignments cannot turn at a sharp point. A curve joins two straights while keeping the change of direction smooth, and chainage carries distance along it. The simple circular curve fixes the geometry; a transition spiral lets curvature and superelevation grow from zero; a vertical parabola joins gradients. Every point on these curves is set out from the tangent using an offset or a deflection angle computed from the radius. Surveyors stake these points for construction, and the same geometry is checked on drawings before a paver or a rail welding gang reaches site.
prereq: You need: chainage and offsets from Unit 1, deflection angles from Chapter 4.2, and fast detail setting out from Chapter 4.4.

sections.h3: Simple circular curve: elements and chainage

blocks.text: Two straights meet at the intersection point I with deflection angle Δ, the angle by which the forward direction turns. A circular arc of radius R joins them. The tangent length T runs from I back to the first tangent point T₁; the curve length L_c runs along the arc; the long chord LC joins T₁ and T₂; E is the external distance from I to the crown; M is the mid-ordinate from the long chord to the crown.
T = R tan(Δ/2), L_c = πRΔ/180, LC = 2R sin(Δ/2), E = R(sec(Δ/2) − 1), M = R(1 − cos(Δ/2))
blocks.where: T is tangent length in m; R radius in m; Δ deflection angle in degrees; L_c curve length (arc) in m; LC long chord in m; E external distance in m; M mid-ordinate in m; sec θ = 1/cos θ.

blocks.text: Chainage follows the route. Chainage of T₁ = chainage of I − T; chainage of T₂ = chainage of I + T; crown chainage = T₁ + L_c/2. A surveyor stakes T₁ and T₂ before any offset.
Degree of curve by the arc definition: D is the central angle subtended by a 100 m arc, so R = 5729.58/D. D is an angle in degrees; R is a length in metres. A smaller D is a flatter curve.

sections.h3: Setting out by offsets and deflection angles

blocks.text: Offsets from the tangent are measured perpendicular from the straight at distance x from T₁: y = R − √(R² − x²) ≈ x²/(2R). The approximation is the parabola used for small x. Offsets from the long chord use x measured from the chord midpoint: y = √(R² − x²) − √(R² − (LC/2)²).

Rankine's deflection method: set the theodolite at T₁, set zero on I, and turn a deflection δ for each point. For a chord c from T₁, δ = c/(2R) radians = 1718.87 c/R minutes. The final deflection to T₂ is Δ/2; the procedure is in Chapter 4.2. A total station computes coordinates of each point and stakes them; the tape and offset become a check. See Unit 5.
For a circular curve, the curve lies wholly between the two tangents, so every offset is measured inward from the straight.

sections.h3: Transition curve: from straight to circle

blocks.text: Curvature cannot jump from zero on the straight to 1/R on the circle. Centrifugal acceleration V²/R (force per unit mass of the vehicle) and superelevation would jump at the tangent point. A transition curve makes curvature grow linearly with distance l: at distance l the radius is R_l, so R_l l = R L_s. At l = 0 it is straight; at l = L_s the radius is R. The clothoid (spiral) does this; for small l its offset is the cubic parabola y = l³/(6 R L_s). A lemniscate is an alternative. The figure uses R = 150 m and transition length L_s = 50 m.
R_l l = R L_s, L_s = V³/(C R), s = L_s²/(24 R)
blocks.where: R_l is radius at distance l in m; R circular radius in m; L_s transition length in m; V speed in m/s; C rate of change of radial acceleration in m/s³; s shift in m; V²/R is the centrifugal acceleration (force per unit mass) in m/s².

blocks.text: Cant gives the same length: equilibrium superelevation e = V²/(gR), with g = 9.81 m/s², and the cant is ramped at a permitted rate. e = V²/(gR) is a ratio with no unit; the outer edge is raised by e × carriageway width, or by e × gauge for rail. Shift s moves the circular arc inward. With equal transitions, tangent length from I to the first tangent point = (R + s) tan(Δ/2) + L_s/2. A sharper curve, a smaller R, needs a longer transition.

A vertical curve joins two gradients g₁ and g₂, written as decimals with sign. Values of g are taken algebraically with sign, so +0.02 means a 2% rise and −0.01 means a 1% fall. A summit falls (g₂ < g₁); a valley rises (g₂ > g₁). A parabola gives constant rate of change of grade.
L_v = |N| / r, c = N x² / (2 L_v)
blocks.where: N = g₂ − g₁ is the algebraic change of grade; r is permitted grade change per metre; c is tangent correction in m; x is distance from start of vertical curve in m; L_v vertical curve length in m.

blocks.text: Length by rate of change of grade is L_v = |N|/r. A second check comes from stopping sight distance: a summit must let the driver see an object over the crest; a valley must keep headlights on the road. At distance x from the start, RL on curve = RL of tangent at that chainage + c. At the start c = 0 and it grows with x; the sign follows N. Set out by chainage and level.

figure.caption: Offsets from the tangent: the parabolic approximation x²/(2R) for a circular curve of radius 150 m, and a cubic transition of length 50 m. The transition rises slowly, so curvature and cant can grow without a jump.

spec.aria: Two curves from the same tangent point: the parabolic approximation for the circular curve climbs to about 8.3 m at 50 m, while the cubic transition climbs to only about 2.8 m.

examples.question: A circular curve of radius R = 300 m deflects an alignment by Δ = 40°. The intersection point is at chainage 2450.000 m. Find T, L_c, long chord, E, M, chainages of T₁ and T₂, and the transition length for design speed 80 km/h with C = 0.3 m/s³.
examples.check:
import math
R = 300.0
Delta = 40.0
chain = 2450.0
V = 80.0/3.6
C = 0.3
T = R*math.tan(math.radians(Delta/2))
L = math.pi*R*Delta/180.0
LC = 2*R*math.sin(math.radians(Delta/2))
E = R*(1/math.cos(math.radians(Delta/2)) - 1)
M = R*(1 - math.cos(math.radians(Delta/2)))
T1 = chain - T
T2 = chain + T
Lt = V**3/(C*R)
for v in (T, L, LC, E, M, T1, T2, Lt):
    print(f'{v:.2f}')

traps: Using Δ where Δ/2 belongs. T uses tan(Δ/2), LC uses sin(Δ/2), E uses sec(Δ/2), and M uses cos(Δ/2).
Mixing degree of curve with radius. D is an angle in degrees; R is a length in metres; for a 100 m arc R = 5729.58/D.
Reversing the transition rule. A sharper curve has smaller R and needs a longer transition, because L_s = V³/(C R).
Finding T₁ and T₂ with arc length. Tangent points come from the straight tangent length T, not from L_c.
Dropping the sign in a vertical curve. Use N = g₂ − g₁ algebraically; a summit gives negative correction and a valley gives positive correction.

quiz.q: State the arc definition of degree of curve and the radius relation.
quiz.a: D is the central angle subtended by a 100 m arc. R = 5729.58/D, with D in degrees and R in metres.

quiz.q: Why is a transition curve needed between a straight and a circular arc?
quiz.a: Curvature would jump from zero to 1/R at the tangent point, so centrifugal force and superelevation would also jump. The transition ramps curvature and cant over a length, removing the jerk.

quiz.q: A circular curve has R = 250 m and Δ = 50°. Find the tangent length.
Find the transition length for V = 60 km/h, R = 200 m and C = 0.4 m/s³.
Why does a smaller radius need a longer transition for the same speed and C?
quiz.a: L_s = V³/(C R), so L_s rises as R falls. A smaller radius means larger curvature and larger radial acceleration, so the change must be spread over a longer distance.

quiz.q: A vertical curve has g₁ = +2%, g₂ = −1%, L_v = 120 m. At x = 60 m the tangent RL is 100.000 m. Find the correction and the curve RL.

beyond: Not for the exam. Road design software builds alignments from clothoids, not circular arcs alone, because a spiral is the path a driver naturally follows. Railway transition curves use the same geometry to limit jerk. Machine control on excavators and pavers uses GNSS coordinates with the same chainage-and-offset logic. Search for clothoid parameter, vertical curve K value, and transition length by cant gradient.
